title: Why It's Getting Harder to Buy a Gift Card
description: Now that retailers are on the hook for fraudulent credit card purchases, supermarkets are making it harder to buy gift cards. WSJ's Robin Sidel reports. asr.full_text: Gift cards are a favorite among criminals who love to buy them with stolen credit card data. So now the credit card industry is holding some merchants liable for this fraud if they haven't updated their checkout technology. As a result, more retailers are making those gift cards harder to come by, with some stores even requiring they be purchased with cash. Here with the story is WSJ Banking Reporter Robin Seidel. Robin, thanks so much for being with us. Sure thing. So gift cards are certainly popular with Americans, correct? And they continue to be even more and more popular. Yes. And this story is specifically about what's called general purpose cards, the ones that are not for specific stores, but for Visa, MasterCard, American Express gift cards. And they're popular as gifts. And people also buy them for themselves. Yes. And there's someone in your story that buys them to pay off his mortgage. Right. Because you can't pay a mortgage with a credit card. So he uses a third-party vendor. So he's still using a credit card to buy the gift card to pay the mortgage. Very interesting use of gift cards. I didn't even know that. Tell us now, why are merchants and retailers being squeezed by the credit card companies. Exactly over these gift cards? So starting in October, there was a liability shift. And previously, the credit card companies are the ones that paid for any fraud on a. Card. And now that's switched to the merchants. And the merchants now bear the responsibility. And so because of that, merchants are upgrading their technology to accept the new chip cards. A lot of merchants are slow doing that, particularly grocery stores. And grocery stores are where a lot of these gift cards are purchased. And so they're making it tougher for people to buy them because they don't want to be on the hook for the fraud. Absolutely. And so give us a sense of how big the fraud is from criminals who buy these gift cards with fake credit card data or stolen credit card data. So there's about $4 billion a year in fraud that comes from counterfeit cards. And a chunk of that is definitely gift cards because they are just the perfect tool for criminals. And criminals have been using them for years. And it's not a problem with the gift cards themselves. It's how they're buying them, the stolen credit cards. So it's just one more step to remove the criminal from the stolen credit card data. It makes it harder to trace and all the rest of it. So now what are some of the ways that retailers are restricting these cards? And who are the major retailers doing that? Well, so far we know Kroger and Safeway are both putting in restrictions. So are some other smaller chains and some others may implement their own. And they're doing all kinds of things. They may be, as you mentioned, prohibiting people from buying a gift card with a credit card. Because they don't want to take that risk and requiring cash. Or they're looking for additional identification when you buy it. Or some of them are actually taking off some of the higher denomination cards from their shelves,. Thinking that those are the ones, $500 cards, that the criminals will gravitate to. Sure, that makes perfect sense. Now, if the merchants do upgrade their checkout technology to include the chip cards,. Will they then still be held liable by the credit card industry,. Or is it just the merchants who haven't upgraded their technology? It's just the merchants who haven't upgraded them. And if the consumer has a chip card and the merchant has a chip machine,. That will reduce counterfeit fraud. Right. And so, you know, increasingly they're adopting it, but just it's complicated and it's expensive. And so it's a big deal for merchants. Something to keep in mind if you do a lot of gift card shopping over the Christmas holidays, right, Robin? Thank you so much for that. You're welcome.
